title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
short_intro: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that a change in magnetic flux linked with a closed circuit induces an electromotive force (emf) in it. The magnitude of the induced emf is directly proportional to the time rate of change of magnetic flux.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of induced emf, magnetic flux, Lenz's law, and Faraday's law for single-turn and multi-turn coils in uniform magnetic fields.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Integral and differential forms of Faraday's law (Maxwell-Faraday equation), motional emf in non-uniform fields, and rotating coils producing alternating emf.

prerequisites: Definition and calculation of magnetic flux (Phi = B dot A)
Vector calculus fundamentals (Line integrals and surface integrals)
Lorentz magnetic force on moving charges

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Flux and Flux Linkage
bullets: Magnetic flux through an elemental surface dS is given by the scalar product of magnetic field B and area vector dS.
For a coil of N turns, the total magnetic flux linkage is defined as N times the magnetic flux linked with a single turn.
The SI unit of magnetic flux is Weber (Wb) or Tesla-meter squared (T·m<sup>2</sup>).

concept_notes.heading: Faraday's First and Second Laws
bullets: First Law: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a closed circuit changes, an electric current (and hence an emf) is induced in it.
Second Law: The magnitude of the induced electromotive force is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage with time.
The dimensional formula of magnetic flux is [M<sup>1</sup> L<sup>2</sup> T<sup>-2</sup> A<sup>-1</sup>].

concept_notes.heading: Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy
bullets: Lenz's law states that the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to oppose the very cause (change in magnetic flux) that produces it.
The negative sign in Faraday's law equation mathematically incorporates Lenz's law.
Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of energy applied to electromagnetic induction.

concept_notes.heading: Motional Electromotive Force (Motional emf)
bullets: When a conductor of length l moves with a velocity v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B, an emf is induced across its ends.
The physical origin of motional emf is the Lorentz magnetic force acting on the free electrons inside the moving conductor.
The induced emf causes a redistribution of charges creating an internal electric field until electrostatic and magnetic forces balance.

derivations.title: Derivation of Induced emf from Magnetic Flux Change
derivations.conditions: A closed loop enclosing a time-varying magnetic flux Phi(t).
steps: Let the magnetic flux linked with a single turn of a coil at time t be Phi<sub>1</sub> and at time t + dt be Phi<sub>2</sub>.
The change in flux during time interval dt is given by dPhi = Phi<sub>2</sub> - Phi<sub>1</sub>.
According to Faraday's second law, the magnitude of induced emf e is proportional to dPhi/dt.
Introducing the negative sign for Lenz's law, the equation becomes e = -N(dPhi/dt) for a coil of N turns.

derivations.title: Derivation of Motional emf for a Rod Moving in a Magnetic Field
derivations.conditions: A straight conductor of length l moving with velocity v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B.
steps: Consider a conducting rod of length l moving to the right with velocity v in a uniform magnetic field B pointing into the page.
A free charge q inside the rod experiences a magnetic force F_m = qvB directed along the length of the rod.
The work done in moving a charge q from one end of the rod to the other is W = F_m · l = qvBl.
Since emf is defined as work done per unit charge, e = W/q = Blv.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnet and Coil Relative Motion Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bar magnet moving towards a closed solenoid connected to a galvanometer, showing deflection.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: A faster approach velocity of the magnet produces a larger galvanometer deflection, confirming that induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually to verify polarity and magnitude dependence on speed and direction of motion.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Induced emf vs Time for Rotating Coil
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sinusoidal curve plotting induced emf e(t) versus time t with peaks at +NωBA and -NωBA.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the generation of alternating voltage via electromagnetic induction as the angle between area vector and magnetic field changes continuously.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in relation to AC generator principles and phase differences between flux and emf.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetic Flux vs Time Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A non-linear curve of flux Phi versus time t, where the slope at any point represents the instantaneous induced emf.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The instantaneous induced emf at any instant is equal in magnitude to the slope of the tangent drawn to the Phi-t curve at that instant.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical graphical analysis where students must calculate induced emf from slope values.

solved_numericals.question: A circular coil of 500 turns and mean diameter 0.1 m is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T normal to the coil plane. If the magnetic field is reduced to zero in 0.02 seconds, find the average induced emf in the coil.
solution_steps: Calculate radius r = diameter / 2 = 0.05 m. Area A = pi * r^2 = 3.1416 * (0.05)^2 = 7.854 * 10^-3 m^2.
Initial magnetic flux Phi_i = B_i * A = 0.4 * 7.854 * 10^-3 = 3.1416 * 10^-3 Wb.
Final magnetic flux Phi_f = 0 Wb. Change in flux Delta Phi = 3.1416 * 10^-3 Wb.
Apply Faraday's law: e = N * (Delta Phi / dt) = 500 * (3.1416 * 10^-3) / 0.02 = 78.54 V.

solved_numericals.question: A metal rod of length 1.0 m rotates with a uniform angular velocity of 20 rad/s about an axis passing through one end and perpendicular to the rod. The rod is immersed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T directed parallel to the axis of rotation. What is the induced emf across the ends of the rod?
solution_steps: Identify the orientation: The magnetic field B is parallel to the axis of rotation.
The component of the magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of rotation (or perpendicular to the length and velocity vector) determines the motional emf.

Here, the magnetic field vector is parallel to the rotation axis, meaning the angle between B and the area swept by the rod is 0 degrees, but the velocity vector of any point on the rod is perpendicular to B and the radial vector.

Wait, let's re-verify: If B is parallel to the axis of rotation, B is perpendicular to the plane swept by the rod. Therefore, the magnetic field is perpendicular to the length and velocity of every element of the rod.
Formula for rotating rod: e = 0.5 * B * omega * l^2 = 0.5 * 0.5 * 20 * (1.0)^2 = 5.0 V.

solved_numericals.question: The magnetic flux passing through a circuit of resistance 10 ohms varies with time t according to the relation Phi = 6t^2 - 5t + 1, where Phi is in Webers and t is in seconds. Find the total charge that passes through any cross-section of the circuit during the time interval t = 0 to t = 2 seconds.
solution_steps: Find the expression for induced current: I(t) = (1/R) * e(t) = -(1/R) * (dPhi/dt).
Differentiate flux with respect to time: dPhi/dt = d/dt (6t^2 - 5t + 1) = 12t - 5.
Integrate current from t = 0 to t = 2 to find total charge Q = integral of I(t) dt from 0 to 2.
Magnitude of charge Q = (1/R) * Delta Phi = (1/10) * [Phi(2) - Phi(0)].
Calculate Phi(2) = 6(2)^2 - 5(2) + 1 = 24 - 10 + 1 = 15 Wb. Calculate Phi(0) = 1 Wb.

assumptions_and_limitations: Faraday's law in its elementary algebraic form assumes lumped parameters and uniform fields over macroscopic areas.
The quasi-stationary approximation is assumed, meaning displacement currents are neglected in standard electromagnetic induction derivations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A stationary conductor in a uniform, time-constant magnetic field can have an induced emf if placed at an angle.
common_misconceptions.correct: No emf is induced in a stationary conductor unless the magnetic flux changes with time.
common_misconceptions.why: Induction strictly requires a time rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Lenz's law opposes the magnetic flux itself.
common_misconceptions.correct: Lenz's law opposes the *change* in magnetic flux, not the magnetic flux itself.
common_misconceptions.why: If flux is constant (even if large), no induced emf is produced.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Induced emf depends on the resistance of the loop.
common_misconceptions.correct: Induced emf depends only on the rate of change of magnetic flux; resistance affects only the induced current.
common_misconceptions.why: Emf is the source term (open-circuit voltage); current is a derived quantity determined by Ohm's law (I = e/R).

quick_revision: Induced emf magnitude is proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage: e = -N(dPhi/dt).
Magnetic Flux: \Phi = \int B \cdot dS = B A \cos\theta
